sections.h2: What should a Dearborn homeowner know before selling?
sections.html:
Dearborn sellers face one step that most Michigan sellers never see: the city requires a Certificate of Occupancy before a house can close. It comes from a city inspection, and it is issued in the buyer's name, so the timing has to be planned from the day you decide to sell.

Dearborn is an inner-ring suburb in Wayne County that borders Detroit on the north and east, about seven miles west of downtown Detroit. The city covers roughly 24.5 square miles and grew up on both banks of the Rouge River. The neighboring village of Fordson, once called Springwells, merged with Dearborn in a 1928 vote.

The Ford Motor Company world headquarters, the Ford River Rouge complex and The Henry Ford museum campus shape the local housing market. Many owners here live close to a Ford job, a hospital or one of the two colleges, and buyers often start their search with commute time.

sections.h2: How does the Dearborn pre-sale inspection work?
sections.html:
The seller, the listing agent or a legally appointed power of attorney files a residential inspection request with the city's Economic Development Department and pays the fee with it. City staff then call to set the visit, which takes about 45 minutes. An adult aged 18 or older must be home for the whole inspection.

The inspector checks basic safety and property maintenance against the city's minimum housing standards, then issues a written report. Every item on that report counts as a code violation and has to be fixed and re-inspected. The sequence runs like this:

  • Submit the application and payment.
  • Wait for staff to schedule the inspection.
  • Be present for the walk-through and keep the report.
  • Correct each listed item within one year of the first inspection date.
  • Request a re-inspection and pass it.
  • Email the buyer's name to the city sales address and say whether the buyer will live in the house, so the certificate can be prepared.

An inspection report stays valid for one year, so a house that falls out of contract can be relisted without starting over, provided the year has not run out.

sections.h2: How does Dearborn housing measure up on paper?
sections.html:
Dearborn leans toward owners and bigger households. These figures come from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts page for the city and cover 2020 to 2024 unless the row says otherwise.

The 2025 estimate sits about 4 percent under the 2020 count. An average household of 2.92 people is well above the 2.43 reported for Detroit and the 2.18 for East Lansing, so buyers here often want extra bedrooms and a usable basement.

sections.h2: Which schools, employers and roads matter to Dearborn buyers?
sections.html:
Dearborn Public Schools operates 34 schools and serves more than 18,000 students, making it the fourth-largest district in Michigan. The main high schools are Fordson High School, Dearborn High School and Edsel Ford High School. Private and charter options include Divine Child, Henry Ford Academy inside Greenfield Village, and Advanced Technology Academy.

The University of Michigan-Dearborn and Henry Ford College sit next to each other on Evergreen Road. Ford is the largest employer by a wide margin in the 2022 annual report the city files, followed by Beaumont Health and the school district. Carhartt, AAA Michigan and Cleveland-Cliffs Dearborn Works also appear among the top ten.

Buyers who commute tend to ask about travel time, and the Census lists a mean of 21.7 minutes for Dearborn workers. Fairlane Town Center, the Henry Ford Centennial Library and the Fair Lane estate give the city's middle section a lot of green and civic space, much of it kept open on land Henry Ford once assembled.

sections.h2: How do Dearborn property taxes work for a seller?
sections.html:
Dearborn sends two bills a year, and each carries different taxing bodies. Whichever bill is open at your closing decides what the settlement statement shows.

  • The summer bill is levied July 1 and due September 14. It holds the school tax, the city tax and the county-allocated operating tax, and an owner can pay it in three pieces (September 14, November 14, January 14) for a one-time $3 charge.
  • The winter bill is levied December 1 and due February 14. The county's remaining levies and the city's combined sewer overflow debt ride on it, and the whole amount is paid at once.
  • Before closing, ask the Treasury Division for a written payoff so the title company pays the right amount.

The cashier counter is at the Dearborn Administrative Center, 16901 Michigan Avenue, weekdays from 8 in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon. The Assessment Department shares the building and answers value questions at 313-943-2140.

sections.h2: What costs and filings come with a Dearborn sale?
sections.html:
Michigan puts the transfer tax on the seller. On every $500 block of sale value the state takes $3.75 (MCL 207.525), and Wayne County adds its own levy under MCL 207.504, which sets 55 cents per block in counties under two million residents. Ask the Wayne County Register of Deeds for the county figure before you build a net sheet.

MCL 207.526 carves out some deeds. Dearborn owners most often meet the exemption for a spouse's deed that creates or ends a tenancy by the entireties, and the one for a land contract whose legal title has not yet passed.

After closing, the buyer notifies the assessor within 45 days (MCL 211.27a). The city's assessment guide describes the next step: in the year after a sale the taxable value is set equal to the state equalized value, and the inflation cap starts again the year after that. If you held a principal residence exemption, ask the Dearborn assessor for the form that removes it.

sections.h2: Which selling route fits a Dearborn house with open inspection items?
sections.html:
A listed sale usually brings the highest price but makes you finish every cited repair before closing. An investor who plans to renovate or rent the house faces the same certificate requirement, and the city asks whether the buyer intends to live there. A private sale lets you and the buyer agree in writing on who pays for corrections, which helps when the inspection list is long.

A long list is the usual reason a Dearborn sale slips. Book the inspection early, settle in writing who handles each correction, and keep the report in your closing file.

faqs.q: Is a city inspection required before my Dearborn house can close?
faqs.a: Yes. Dearborn requires a Certificate of Occupancy before closing, and it comes after a pre-sale inspection. You, your agent or a power of attorney requests the visit, fixes any violations, passes a re-inspection and then emails the buyer's name to city staff so the certificate is issued in that name.

faqs.q: How long is a Dearborn inspection report valid?
faqs.a: One year from the date of the first inspection. You have that same year to correct every listed violation and pass the re-inspection, so a sale that falls through does not force a second full inspection if you relist inside the year.

faqs.q: When are Dearborn property taxes due?
faqs.a: Summer taxes are due September 14 and winter taxes are due February 14. Summer taxes can be paid in three installments on September 14, November 14 and January 14, while winter taxes must be paid in full.

faqs.q: Who pays the state transfer tax in a Dearborn sale?
faqs.a: The seller. Michigan makes the grantor liable, at $3.75 per $500 of value for the state plus the Wayne County levy. A few deeds are exempt, such as a spouse's deed creating a tenancy by the entireties.

faqs.q: What happens to the tax bill once I sell?
faqs.a: It rises for the buyer in most cases. The year after a sale, taxable value becomes equal to state equalized value, and the inflation cap applies again from the following year. Your own exemption ends when you rescind it with the assessor.
